title: Cheap Desktop 400GbE Switch MikroTik CRS804-4DDQ-hRM Review
gist: MikroTik's CRS804-4DDQ-hRM packs 4x400GbE (1.6Tbps) into a half-width desktop switch at roughly $0.70/Gbps street price, and the reviewer is already running it as RDMA backend fabric for small NVIDIA GB10 and GB300 Station AI clusters, signaling that high-speed AI-networking gear is becoming affordable at lab/desktop scale.

insights.claim: The MikroTik CRS804-4DDQ-hRM lists at $1295 but commonly sells at a street price around $1100, working out to under $0.70 per Gbps of switching capacity.
insights.speaker: Rohit Kumar
insights.so_what: Sub-$1/Gbps pricing for 400GbE marks a step-change in cost for high-speed AI/RDMA networking gear, lowering the entry barrier for labs and small clusters versus enterprise switch vendors.
insights.quote: The list price is $1295, but these often sell at a street price of $1100 or so, making this under $0.70/Gbps.

insights.claim: The reviewer frames the switch's cost efficiency by comparing it to legacy 1GbE gear, noting the $/Gbps is equivalent to an 8-port 1GbE switch costing $5.50 per Gbps.
insights.speaker: Rohit Kumar
insights.so_what: Using $/Gbps as the yardstick (rather than absolute price) reframes 400GbE switching as cheap infrastructure, useful for modeling AI cluster networking capex per unit of bandwidth.
insights.quote: Putting that into perspective, it is like an 8-port 1GbE switch for only $5.50 per Gbps.

insights.claim: Despite the low $/Gbps, the switch is in high demand and hard to source, with the reviewer's units purchased from B&H.
insights.speaker: Rohit Kumar
insights.so_what: Supply tightness on a budget 400GbE switch suggests demand for affordable AI-cluster networking is outstripping availability, a leading indicator for the broader lab/prosumer AI infrastructure buildout.
insights.quote: If you want to purchase these, they are in high demand, but we bought ours from B&H

insights.claim: The switch provides four QSFP56-DD ports totaling 1.6Tbps of switching capacity, and each port can be split into 2x200GbE QSFP56 connections for more granular fan-out.
insights.speaker: Rohit Kumar
insights.so_what: Port-splitting flexibility lets buyers trade four 400GbE links for up to eight 200GbE links, widening the switch's applicability across mixed-speed AI/RDMA fabrics without buying additional hardware.

insights.claim: The CRS804 uses QSFP56-DD ports, which are distinct from the QSFP112 ports found on NVIDIA's GB300 Station and the OSFP ports used in higher-end switches like NVIDIA's Spectrum-X series and many ConnectX-8/ConnectX-9 cards, meaning DACs and optics must be QSFP56-DD-specific.
insights.speaker: Rohit Kumar
insights.so_what: Optics/cabling ecosystems are fragmented by connector type (QSFP56-DD vs QSFP112 vs OSFP), so buyers must plan transceiver and DAC compatibility carefully when mixing this switch with NVIDIA-class AI networking gear.
insights.quote: These are not the QSFP112 ports you would find in something like the NVIDIA GB300 station... These are not the OSFP ports you would find in higher-end switches like the NVIDIA Spectrum-X series or many ConnectX-8/ ConnectX-9 cards.

insights.claim: The switch is a half-width unit (218mm wide, 387mm deep) with redundant hot-swappable 350W Gospower power supplies and hot-swappable fans, though its depth makes dense side-by-side lab mounting difficult.
insights.speaker: Rohit Kumar
insights.so_what: Enterprise-grade redundancy (dual hot-swap PSUs and fans) at this price point signals the switch targets always-on lab/edge AI deployments, not just hobbyist use, though physical depth constrains rack density.

insights.claim: The reviewer has been running one CRS804-4DDQ-hRM as the RDMA network backend for an 8x NVIDIA GB10 cluster for several months, and a second unit for an NVIDIA GB300 Station cluster using DR4 optics.
insights.speaker: Rohit Kumar
insights.so_what: Direct production use as RDMA fabric for both a GB10-class and GB300-class NVIDIA AI cluster validates that budget 400GbE switching is already good enough for real small-scale AI training/inference backends, not just a spec-sheet claim.
insights.quote: We have a number of these now and have been running our RDMA network backend for the 8x NVIDIA GB10 cluster for several months now, using one.

insights.claim: The affordability and availability of 1.6Tbps desktop switches implies that high-bandwidth RDMA fabric is becoming commoditized down to the small-cluster and lab scale, not just hyperscale data centers.
insights.speaker: Rohit Kumar
insights.so_what: As 400GbE switching commoditizes, the cost floor for standing up a small RDMA-connected AI cluster drops, potentially widening the base of organizations and individuals who can build competitive local AI infrastructure.
